extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century periodical readers; educated public interested in morals, manners, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Producing short moral, social, and literary essays (Spectator-style) addressed to a general educated readership, combining satire, practical moral counsel, and literary criticism. Pieces mix prescriptive social guidance with concrete examples and occasional literary analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity founded on frugality
rubrics_metrics.description: All Liberality should have for its Basis and Support Frugality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give so as to secure the ability to continue doing good: beneficence should proceed from reason not impulse; avoid reducing one's fortune below the capacity to act according to one's temper. Example: do not sacrifice future opportunities to help by rash largesse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate public largesses by circumstance and fortune
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses to the People by Largesses and publick Entertainments ... are in general vicious, and are always to be regulated according to the Circumstances of Time and a Man's own Fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ostentatious public entertainments that exceed one's means or the demands of the time; generosity should not be performative if it undermines prudence or invites censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant benignity in commercial life
rubrics_metrics.description: A constant Benignity in Commerce with the rest of the World ... has Effects more useful to those whom you oblige, and less ostentatious in your self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In trade be frank in kindnesses, just and easy in buying, selling, lending; be averse to disputes and petty severity. Such steady benignity does more good than isolated public displays of generosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion in bestowing favors (keep favors secret)
rubrics_metrics.description: He who obliges is as much concerned to keep the Favour a Secret, as he who receives it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conceal generous acts to avoid creating enemies, envy, or invidious distinctions; secrecy protects both giver and recipient and preserves social harmony. Example: Tom the Bounteous conceals his compassion under a rough air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer aiding humble, industrious people
rubrics_metrics.description: What you do to a Man of an humble Fortune ... raises the Affections towards you of all Men of that Character ... in the whole City.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assisting modest, industrious persons produces wider gratitude and social benefit than aiding the conspicuous; such support extends a man's benignity furthest within civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support public funds/state as a form of civic generosity
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Nation where there are so many publick Funds to be supported ... he who does not imbark some part of his Fortune with the State ... can hardly be called a good Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investing part of one's fortune in public or state funds is a patriotic way to lay obligations on many and extend one's beneficence beyond private commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify authenticity before publishing sensational accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: I am in some doubt whether the following Pieces are Genuine and Authentick; and the more so, because I am not fully satisfied that the Name by which the Emperor subscribes himself, is altogether conformable to the Indian Orthography. ... I did not think fit to publish them till now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should exercise caution and verify authenticity (names, facts) before printing sensational or alarming material; delay publication when in doubt to avoid spreading false panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid detraction and diminishing praise-worthy persons
rubrics_metrics.description: This impertinent Humour of diminishing every one who is produced in Conversation to their Advantage runs thro the World ... Merit ... is become no other than the Possession of a few trifling Peoples Favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist the habit of pulling down those who receive praise; suppressing commendation discourages talent and makes deserving people conceal their gifts. Encourage recognition rather than malicious diminution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary that praise can provoke malicious scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: I have begged of all those who are my Well-wishers never to commend me, for it will but bring my Frailties into Examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account that public commendation may invite envy and the exposure of faults; weigh the social consequences of praising someone prominently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay definitive praise until after death (reputation sealed by death)
rubrics_metrics.description: Death only closes a Man's Reputation, and determines it as good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in declaring a person's life virtuous or vicious while they live, because later actions can alter judgment; death fixes reputation in a way life does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value constancy of character through life
rubrics_metrics.description: There is nothing more glorious than to keep up an Uniformity in his Actions, and preserve the Beauty of his Character to the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral greatness by the maintenance of uniform virtue over a lifetime; examples (Sir Thomas More, Socrates) show consistent behavior at death confirms character.

rubrics_metrics.name: True courage must include justice and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: Courage, without regard to Justice and Humanity, was no other than the Fierceness of a wild Beast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bravery divorced from justice becomes mere ferocity; genuine magnanimity couples boldness with reason, honour, and concern for right conduct. Example: contrast the brave defence of Goodwin with the privateer's vengeful cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modesty as the sign of great spirit; impudence is affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Modesty is the certain Indication of a great Spirit, and Impudence the Affectation of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge true greatness by modest, measured comportment rather than noisy self-assertion; those who are quiet and equal in behaviour demonstrate genuine gallantry, whereas loudness often signals affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge valor by conduct and success, not mere display
rubrics_metrics.description: If Equipage and Address make Turnus appear more couragious than Æneas, Conduct and Success prove Æneas more valiant than Turnus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External show (equipage, address) can create appearance of bravery, but real valor is demonstrated by actions, consequences, and other virtues (e.g., piety).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poets should incorporate traditional particulars and preserve character
rubrics_metrics.description: He has interwoven, in the course of his Fable, the principal Particulars, which were generally believed among the Romans, of Æneas his Voyage and Settlement in Italy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When poetical subject rests on scant historical material, retain and weave in the main traditional particulars and established character traits to root the poem in received belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt ludicrous traditional elements so they fit the epic tone
rubrics_metrics.description: That ludicrous Prophecy ... that before they had built their intended City, they should be reduced by Hunger to eat their very Tables ... Virgil qualified it so as to make it appear proper: the Prophetess is a Hungry Harpy, and the person who discovers it is young Ascanius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tradition contains odd or comic incidents, qualify them by appropriate narrative devices (make the speaker an unlikely or comic figure, place it in the mouth of a child) to render them acceptable within an elevated genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use invention to circumstantiate sparse historical material
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet took the matters of Fact as they came down to him, and circumstanced them after his own manner, to make them appear the more natural, agreeable, or surprizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where historical detail is scant, the poet may invent or embellish incidents to fill out the narrative, shaping facts to achieve naturalness and pleasure for the reader while preserving principal traditions.
